title: Did Material Properties Contribute to the 1284 Collapse of Beauvais Cathedral? A Comparative Assessment of Stone Masonry, Mortar Behaviour and Structural Vulnerability
content: The partial collapse of the choir vaults of Beauvais Cathedral in 1284 has been explained through structural and constructional hypotheses, but the role of the materials has never been tested against laboratory data. This study assesses four material-dependent mechanisms—crushing, differential shortening between coursed masonry and monolithic shafts, time-dependent deformation under eccentric load, and the dependence of the buttressing on stone strength—using a traceable database that combines published tests on the Coniacian chalk of Beauvais, data on air lime mortars, the documented geometry of the choir and field measurements of the masonry bond. Uncertainty is propagated through 10⁵ Monte Carlo simulations. The safety margin of the choir piers against crushing lies between 1.4 and 4.7, far below the values that justified regarding the material as irrelevant. Coursed masonry shortens 3.9 to 6.0 times more than a monolithic shaft in the long term, whereas creep-induced amplification in the main piers is small. The results indicate that the material did not cause the collapse through lack of strength, but contributed to it through its deformability and its sensitivity to water.
